pages.text: Aesop was a storyteller who lived in ancient Greece approximately 2,600 years ago. Almost nothing certain is known about his life. Some accounts say he was a slave who won his freedom through his intelligence and wit. Others say he was born in Africa. Almost all agree that he was famous throughout the ancient world for his stories, the short, sharp tales we now call fables.

image.note: Illustration: a man seated beneath an olive tree, animals gathered around him attentively

pages.text: A fable is a very short story that ends with a moral: a statement of a lesson about how to live. Aesop's fables use animals as characters. The animals behave like people, making the same mistakes, falling for the same tricks, suffering the same pride and greed and fear. Because the characters are animals, the lessons feel universal: this is not a story about one person. It is a story about all of us.

Aesop's fables were passed down orally for centuries before being written down. Scholars have debated whether a single person called Aesop wrote all the fables, or whether the name Aesop came to stand for a tradition of short moral stories. It does not much matter. The stories work, whoever told them first. They have been told and retold for 2,600 years because they are true.
A crow found a piece of cheese and flew up to a high branch to eat it. A fox, passing below, looked up and saw the cheese. He wanted it.

image.note: Illustration: a crow on a branch holding cheese in its beak, a fox looking up from below with a calculating expression

pages.text: 'What a magnificent bird you are,' the fox said. 'Your feathers are so black and glossy. Your wings are so strong. I have never seen a more beautiful crow in all my travels.' The crow puffed up with pride. 'I am sure,' the fox went on, 'that a bird as magnificent as you must have a magnificent voice. Would you honour me with a song?' The crow opened its beak to sing. The cheese fell. The fox caught it and ate it. 'Thank you,' he said. 'I have your voice. But I did not need to hear it to know it was your vanity that I was really after.'
Moral: Flattery is a weapon. The person who praises you most loudly may want something from you.

The fox trotted away well pleased, and the crow was left with nothing but the memory of praise. Foolish creature, to lose good food for the sake of a compliment. Yet the fox had told no lie the crow wished to hear less than the truth: the crow's voice was indeed harsh. It was the crow's own vanity, not the fox's cleverness, that opened its beak. The trap was set with flattery, but the crow sprang it.
The hare was the fastest animal in the forest. He knew it. He told everyone about it, frequently.

image.note: Illustration: a hare looking dismissively at a tortoise on a forest path

pages.text: 'Race me if you dare,' he said to the tortoise one morning. The tortoise agreed. The hare ran far ahead in the first minute, looked back, and laughed at the tiny figure plodding along far behind. He lay down in the shade for a sleep. 'I have plenty of time,' he told himself. He slept. The tortoise walked, steadily and without stopping, past the sleeping hare, past the finish line, and waited there for twenty minutes before the hare woke up and realised what had happened.
Moral: Steady, consistent effort beats natural talent that is wasted on arrogance.
This is the story that first appeared at Level 3. Now it is told in full.

image.note: Illustration: a tiny mouse standing on the paw of a sleeping lion in dappled forest light

pages.text: A lion lay sleeping in the sun. A mouse, not noticing, ran across his paw. The lion woke and snatched the mouse up. 'I shall eat you,' he said. 'Please,' said the mouse, 'let me go. I am too small to be a proper meal for a king. And perhaps one day I can repay you.' The lion laughed. He laughed so hard that he let the mouse go, simply because the idea of a mouse repaying a lion was so absurd that he was curious to see if it could possibly be true.

Weeks later, the lion was caught in a net set by hunters. He roared. He struggled. He could not get free. The mouse heard the roaring and came to see. The mouse bit through the ropes of the net, fibre by fibre, until the lion was free. 'You see,' said the mouse. The lion had nothing to say.
Moral: No act of kindness is wasted. No one is too small to matter.

There is another tale of the mouse worth telling. A town mouse once visited his cousin in the country and turned up his nose at the plain meal of grain and roots. Come to town, he said, and taste real living. In the town house the food was rich and plentiful, but twice the meal was interrupted by barking dogs and prowling cats, and each time the two mice fled for their lives. The country mouse packed his bag.

Better beans and safety, said the country mouse at the door, than cakes and terror. He returned to his quiet field, his simple food, and his unhurried sleep, and never envied the town again. The town mouse, for his part, could not understand it. Each mouse, in the end, valued what he was used to. What looks like poverty to one creature is peace to another.

chapters.title: The Boy Who Cried Wolf, and Others

pages.text: A boy was set to watch the village's sheep on the hillside. One afternoon, out of boredom, he ran to the village shouting that a wolf had come. The villagers ran up the hill with sticks and farming tools, found no wolf, and walked back down again, annoyed.

image.note: Illustration: villagers looking frustrated as a boy laughs on a hillside; sheep grazing peacefully

pages.text: The next week, he did it again. The villagers ran up, found nothing, returned in silence. The third time, a wolf actually came. The boy shouted until he was hoarse. Nobody came. The wolf ate several of the sheep. When the boy returned to the village, an elder said to him: 'We didn't come because we thought you were lying again.' 'But I wasn't!' the boy said. 'I know,' said the elder. 'And that is precisely the problem. Your lies were not harmless. They cost you your credibility, and that cost the village its sheep.'
Moral: Truth is valuable because it is reliable. Undermine that reliability and the truth will not be believed even when it matters most.

One more fable belongs here, for it is among the wisest. The wind and the sun argued over which was stronger, and agreed to settle it on a traveller below: whichever could make him remove his coat would win. The wind blew a gale, but the harder it blew, the tighter the traveller clutched his coat against the cold. Then the sun shone warm and gentle, and within minutes the traveller took the coat off himself. Gentleness had done what force could not.

That is the heart of Aesop. The strong are not always those who push hardest. The clever are not always those who shout loudest. Again and again these little stories, told by a man who may have begun life as a slave, quietly favour the patient over the proud, the kind over the cruel, and the wise over the merely powerful. Two and a half thousand years later, the world still needs the reminder.
